transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Mr. Okafor. I wanted to come in and speak with you personally about the imaging and the plan for your surgery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate that. A nurse came by about twenty minutes ago and mentioned there was some sort of mix-up with my MRI. I'm not entirely sure what that means for me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am very sorry. To be direct, we made a serious mistake. Your MRI scan and another patient's scan were stored under the same identification number in our system. Because of that, my team reviewed the wrong images when we were deciding on the approach for your surgery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The wrong images? You mean you were looking at someone else's anatomy while planning my operation?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened. We looked at another person's scan instead of yours. I take full responsibility for this. It is unacceptable, and I apologize deeply for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a retired teacher, so I'm used to mistakes in a classroom, but this is a different league. I'm trying to understand how two different people end up with the same number. Is the system that flawed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in how the data was entered and verified. While there is a software component, we failed to double-check the patient name against the image. I know this is incredibly unsettling to hear.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Unsettling is one word for it. I'm mostly wondering if you've already operated on me based on the wrong pictures.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, we caught the error before any surgical intervention took place. You have not been operated on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Well, thank goodness for that. But it still leaves a bad taste. If you got the images wrong, what else is getting missed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely fair question. It's a frightening realization that the process we trust failed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is. I feel like I can't just trust the "system" now. I need to know exactly how you're going to fix this so I don't end up on the wrong table.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. I want to make sure I've explained this clearly so far. Does the nature of the mix-up make sense, or can I clarify any part of how the images were swapped?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I understand the mechanics. Wrong file, wrong patient, wrong plan. My concern is the remedy.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have a specific three-step plan to ensure your safety moving forward. First, I have personally pulled your correct images and spent the last hour re-reviewing them. Second, I have scheduled a second opinion with the Chief of Surgery for tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to verify the new surgical approach. Third, we have implemented a mandatory "double-verify" step for your specific file, meaning two different doctors must sign off on the image identity before we enter the operating room.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And when will I actually know the final plan?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: After the Chief's review tomorrow morning, I will come back to your room by 11:00 AM to go over the corrected approach with you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll hold you to that time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I am also filing a formal incident report today. Part of that process is a root-cause analysis to figure out why that accession number was duplicated, so we can prevent this from happening to any other patient in this hospital.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate the apology, and I appreciate the plan. I'm still quite annoyed, as I'm sure you can tell.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I don't blame you for being annoyed. It is a failure of our standard of care. I am here for as long as you need if you have more questions, or if you'd like me to call anyone for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think I've had enough for the moment. I'll see you tomorrow at eleven.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be here. I'm truly sorry again, Mr. Okafor.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish all turns, remains regulated under pushback, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the second turn, lay language used throughout, and comprehension checked twice (at 02:14 and 02:25).

A.justification: Direct apologies used multiple times, resident takes full responsibility ('I take full responsibility'), and maintains accountability throughout.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('unsettling', 'frightening', 'annoyed') and references the patient's specific concerns about trust.

T.justification: Specific next steps with timelines are provided (Chief's review tomorrow, 11:00 AM update) and prevention is addressed, but the patient's active role in the plan is not named.
